personal.background:
Alex Kauffman is a designer who graduated with a BFA from {{rit}}. After years of working in digital design, he is shifting his focus toward human factors engineering and human interface design, grounding his work in systems that amplify user cognition rather than automate it.

Outside of work, Alex spends his time riding dirt bikes, snowboarding, and traveling.

personal.coding: Alex thrives at the intersection of design and interface logic, translating human intent into responsive environments. Drawing inspiration from classic computing architecture and command-line interfaces, he values software that demands active participation and clear feedback over black-box automation.
personal.ai_thinking:
I believe AI has real value in science and engineering—especially in areas like protein modeling, vaccine development, and pattern discovery where speed and scale matter.

I’m far less convinced by generative AI as a surrogate for human reasoning. Technology should serve as a bicycle for the mind, not a replacement for it. Older paradigms like CLI systems excel because they keep the user actively thinking and researching.

AI should extend human cognition, surface patterns, and reduce friction—it is not the output. Humans define the intent, context, and meaning. AI is just a tool to amplify our thinking, not replace it.

In the end, the essence of computing depends on human agency.
personal.Favcolor:

A rich, nature-inspired hue that brings an affluent layer to any space or product—striking the perfect antidote to overused millennial gray.
personal.Favproduct:
The product: {{gameboy}}.

The Core Insight: Pure engineering within strict constraints. Today's software often relies on massive RAM, GPUs, and bloated interfaces just to function. The Game Boy proves that when every byte and pixel matters, simplicity wins.

Why it matters to my work: It taught me that we don't need to over-engineer to create impact. With just two input buttons and a monochrome screen, it delivered deep engagement through pure systems thinking. I build with that same respect for performance, efficiency, and intentional design.

Second product:

The Apollo Guidance Computer which uses the core rope memory, where software code was literally woven by hand using copper wires and tiny magnetic rings.
